questions.question: A 65-year-old man is evaluated in the outpatient psychiatry clinic 3 months after discharge following a heart transplant. His hospital course was complicated by cardiogenic shock requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an ICU stay notable for delirium. Since returning home he has had nightly nightmares about the ICU, flashbacks triggered by flashing lights on the television, persistent thoughts that his body is permanently broken, and constant irritability that has caused conflict with his family. He has stopped watching television, which he previously enjoyed. Laboratory studies are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.B: Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
answers.C: Delirium due to another medical condition

explanations.A: Acute stress disorder requires that symptoms be present for 3 days to 1 month after the trauma; his symptoms have persisted for 3 months.
explanations.B: Adjustment disorder is diagnosed only when the presentation does not meet criteria for another disorder, and here the full PTSD symptom cluster following a life-threatening event is present.
explanations.C: His delirium resolved before discharge and his metabolic studies are essentially unremarkable; delirium requires an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness.
explanations.D: Major depressive disorder would center on pervasive low mood and anhedonia rather than trauma-specific nightmares, flashbacks, and cue-driven avoidance.
explanations.E: A life-threatening medical course is a qualifying Criterion A exposure, and he has intrusion (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance (television), negative cognitions ('my body is broken'), and arousal (irritability) lasting more than 1 month.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is evaluated 10 days after she was assaulted while walking home from work. Since the assault she has had intrusive memories of the attack, recurrent nightmares, an inability to feel any happiness, episodes in which she feels as though she is observing herself from outside her body, avoidance of the street where the attack occurred, difficulty falling asleep, an exaggerated startle response, and poor concentration. She has missed work and stopped seeing friends. She has no psychiatric history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: She has at least nine symptoms spanning intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, occurring 3 days to 1 month after a qualifying trauma with functional impairment.
explanations.B: Adjustment disorder is a residual diagnosis used when criteria for a specific disorder are not met, and she meets full acute stress disorder criteria after a life-threatening event.
explanations.C: Brief psychotic disorder requires delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech; her depersonalization is a dissociative rather than psychotic symptom.
explanations.D: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory worry, whereas her symptoms are cued by and centered on a specific traumatic event.
explanations.E: Posttraumatic stress disorder cannot be diagnosed until symptoms have lasted longer than 1 month, and she is only 10 days out from the assault.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for low mood and frequent tearfulness that began 6 weeks ago, shortly after she was unexpectedly laid off from a job she had held for 10 years. She reports difficulty concentrating, worry about finances, and she has stopped attending her weekly book club. She denies anhedonia, appetite or weight change, psychomotor changes, hopelessness, or suicidal ideation, and she has no history of trauma exposure. Her distress is markedly greater than that of colleagues laid off at the same time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Emotional symptoms began within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, are out of proportion to the severity of that stressor, impair functioning, and do not meet criteria for another disorder.
explanations.B: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple domains for at least 6 months, not worry that arises from a single recent identifiable stressor.
explanations.C: Major depressive disorder requires five or more symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia for at least 2 weeks, and she lacks anhedonia, neurovegetative changes, and hopelessness.
explanations.D: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years, whereas her symptoms started 6 weeks ago.
explanations.E: Job loss is not a Criterion A exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, and she reports no intrusion or avoidance symptoms.

questions.question: A 40-year-old accountant is evaluated for nightmares, avoidance behavior, and hypervigilance that began several months ago. She has no military service and does not work as a first responder. Her psychiatrist is determining whether her exposure history satisfies Criterion A for posttraumatic stress disorder. Which of the following exposures would satisfy this criterion?

answers.A: Learning that a close friend was killed in a violent car crash
answers.B: Reading a detailed newspaper account of a mass shooting
answers.C: Repeatedly watching televised footage of a terrorist bombing
answers.D: Scrolling through social media images of a natural disaster
answers.E: Viewing a documentary film about combat in a war zone

explanations.A: Criterion A includes learning that a traumatic event occurred to a close family member or close friend, provided the death was violent or accidental.
explanations.B: Reading a media account is indirect exposure and does not qualify unless the exposure is repeated, extreme, and work related.
explanations.C: Criterion A explicitly excludes exposure through television and other electronic media unless the exposure is work related, which does not apply to an accountant.
explanations.D: Social media images are electronic media exposure and are excluded from Criterion A outside of occupational duties.
explanations.E: Watching a film depicting combat is media exposure to events that did not happen to the patient or a close friend or relative.

questions.question: A 29-year-old veteran with posttraumatic stress disorder participates in a functional neuroimaging study. While listening to a recorded script describing his combat trauma, he reports intense fear and says he cannot stop scanning the room for threats. Which of the following patterns of brain activity is most likely to be observed during the script?

answers.A: Decreased amygdala activity with increased ventromedial prefrontal activity
answers.B: Increased amygdala activity with decreased ventromedial prefrontal activity
answers.C: Increased cerebellar activity with decreased brainstem activity
answers.D: Increased hippocampal activity with decreased amygdala activity
answers.E: Increased occipital activity with decreased thalamic activity

explanations.A: This is the reverse of the established pattern and would predict effective top-down regulation of fear rather than the attentional bias toward threat seen here.
explanations.B: Functional imaging in PTSD shows amygdala and dorsal anterior cingulate hyperreactivity with ventromedial prefrontal hyporeactivity, underlying threat bias, impaired emotion regulation, and persistence of fear memories.
explanations.C: Cerebellar and brainstem changes are not the characteristic imaging signature of PTSD, though brainstem activation contributes to hyperarousal and startle.
explanations.D: The hippocampus in PTSD shows volume loss and impaired memory consolidation rather than hyperactivity, and amygdala activity is increased rather than decreased.
explanations.E: Occipital activation can accompany visual intrusions, but thalamic suppression paired with occipital activation is not the described PTSD pattern.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with posttraumatic stress disorder that developed after a house fire is unable to recall how he escaped the building or the 30 minutes that followed, although he vividly recalls the smell of smoke and the sound of the alarm. Head CT obtained on the night of the fire was normal, and toxicology screening at that time was negative. Dysfunction of which of the following structures best accounts for this finding?

explanations.A: The amygdala attaches emotional valence to threat cues and drives fear responses; its dysfunction produces hyperreactivity, not gaps in autobiographical memory.
explanations.B: The dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is hyperreactive in PTSD and contributes to threat monitoring rather than to encoding and retrieval of episodic memory.
explanations.C: Hippocampal volume loss and disrupted memory consolidation account for the inability to recall an important aspect of the trauma when head injury and substances have been excluded.
explanations.D: Locus ceruleus noradrenergic activation underlies hyperarousal, startle, and autonomic reactivity rather than dissociative amnesia.
explanations.E: Medial orbitofrontal dysfunction is associated with anger, irritability, and recklessness rather than with memory gaps.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man with posttraumatic stress disorder following a roadside bombing is brought in by his wife because over the past several months he has punched walls with minimal provocation and has begun driving at high speeds without a seatbelt. He denies any wish to die and denies suicidal ideation. His memory and orientation are intact. Disruption of which of the following structures best accounts for these symptoms?

explanations.A: The dorsal raphe supplies serotonergic modulation implicated in mood and impulsivity broadly, but it is not the region mapped to these specific behaviors in trauma.
explanations.B: Hippocampal disruption in PTSD manifests as memory impairment, and his memory is intact.
explanations.C: Medial orbitofrontal cortex dysfunction in PTSD maps onto anger, irritability, and reckless or self-destructive behavior, both of which are Criterion E arousal symptoms.
explanations.D: Visual cortex activation is linked to visual intrusions, flashbacks, and hypervigilance rather than aggression and recklessness.
explanations.E: Ventral striatal dysfunction relates to reward processing and anhedonia rather than to angry outbursts with little provocation.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is evaluated 8 months after a sexual assault. She reports intrusive memories, avoidance of reminders, persistent guilt that she should have prevented the assault, hypervigilance, and difficulty falling asleep. She has stopped working. She has never taken a psychiatric medication and would like to start one. Vital signs and laboratory studies are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

explanations.A: Benzodiazepines are considered harmful in PTSD, may worsen symptoms and recovery, and carry dependence risk.
explanations.B: Bupropion falls into the unknown-benefit category for PTSD and lacks evidence supporting its use as initial therapy.
explanations.C: Lithium is used only as an augmenting agent after inadequate response to first-line antidepressant therapy.
explanations.D: Atypical antipsychotic monotherapy has at best limited support in PTSD and is not appropriate for a treatment-naive patient.
explanations.E: Sertraline is an SSRI with FDA approval for PTSD, and SSRIs are the class with the strongest evidence of benefit as first-line pharmacotherapy.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with posttraumatic stress disorder has taken sertraline at a therapeutic dose for 12 weeks. His irritability, avoidance, and daytime anxiety have improved substantially, but he continues to wake three or four nights per week from vivid dreams that replay the motor vehicle collision in which his brother died. He falls asleep easily and his blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

explanations.A: Benzodiazepines are considered harmful in PTSD and do not address trauma nightmares specifically.
explanations.B: Lithium is a general augmentation option for residual PTSD symptoms and has no particular efficacy for nightmares.
explanations.C: Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist, has demonstrated benefit specifically for trauma-related nightmares and sleep disturbance in PTSD.
explanations.D: Atypical antipsychotics are adjunctive options with limited evidence and carry metabolic risk not justified for isolated nightmares.
explanations.E: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics are of unknown benefit in PTSD and target sleep initiation, which is not his problem.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with posttraumatic stress disorder following a home invasion reports severe anxiety and difficulty sleeping. She asks for the medication a friend takes because it 'works right away.' She has a history of alcohol use disorder in remission for 2 years and is currently taking no medications. Which of the following agents is most likely to worsen her long-term outcome?

explanations.A: Clonidine is an adjunctive option of uncertain benefit in PTSD but is not classified as harmful.
explanations.B: Benzodiazepines are classified as harmful in PTSD, may interfere with extinction learning and psychotherapy, and pose a substantial relapse and dependence risk in a patient with a substance use history.
explanations.C: Prazosin is a recognized adjunctive treatment for trauma-related nightmares with a favorable risk profile.
explanations.D: Sertraline is FDA approved for PTSD and is an appropriate first-line agent.
explanations.E: Venlafaxine is an SNRI, a class with demonstrated significant benefit in PTSD.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with acute stress disorder 2 weeks after he was trapped for several hours in a partially collapsed building. He has intrusive memories, dissociative episodes, avoidance of construction sites, and marked insomnia. He asks his physician what is likely to happen over the next several months if the condition is not treated. Approximately what proportion of patients with acute stress disorder go on to develop posttraumatic stress disorder?

explanations.A: This figure is far too low; acute stress disorder is one of the most reliable predictors of subsequent PTSD.
explanations.B: This underestimates the risk and would incorrectly suggest that acute stress disorder rarely progresses.
explanations.C: Approximately one-quarter is the proportion of all major trauma-exposed individuals who develop PTSD, not the proportion of those with acute stress disorder.
explanations.D: About half of patients who meet criteria for acute stress disorder subsequently develop PTSD, which is why early psychotherapeutic intervention is offered.
explanations.E: This overstates the risk; a substantial minority of patients with acute stress disorder recover without progressing to PTSD.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is evaluated for mood lability, anger, and feelings of emptiness that worsened after her boyfriend ended their relationship 2 months ago. Her mother reports that since early adolescence she has had unstable and intense relationships, repeated impulsive decisions, and extreme reactions to any perceived rejection, with nearly identical episodes after every prior breakup. Which of the following features most strongly argues against a diagnosis of adjustment disorder?

answers.A: Anger and emptiness rather than depressed mood alone
answers.B: Onset of symptoms within 3 months of the breakup
answers.C: Persistence of symptoms for longer than 1 month
answers.D: Predominance of an interpersonal rather than life-threatening stressor
answers.E: Similar reactions to rejection dating back to adolescence

explanations.A: Adjustment disorder specifiers include disturbance of conduct and mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, so anger does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanations.B: Onset within 3 months of an identifiable stressor is a required feature of adjustment disorder rather than an argument against it.
explanations.C: Adjustment disorder symptoms may persist while the stressor continues and for up to 6 months after it resolves.
explanations.D: Adjustment disorder is triggered by any identifiable stressor and specifically does not require a life-threatening event.
explanations.E: A lifetime pattern of the same maladaptive reactions points to a personality disorder, whose features have a lifelong history rather than arising in response to a discrete recent stressor.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man is seen in the transplant clinic 4 months after a prolonged hospitalization for cardiogenic shock. He describes nightmares about the ICU, avoidance of the hospital, and constant hypervigilance. His physician reviews the hospital course to identify contributors to his current presentation. Which of the following elements of his hospitalization is an independent risk factor for posttraumatic stress disorder?

answers.A: Discharge to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation
answers.B: Elevated serum creatinine at the time of admission
answers.C: Placement of a peripheral intravenous catheter
answers.D: Prescription of a statin at the time of discharge

explanations.A: Rehabilitation placement reflects functional status and has not been identified as an independent driver of trauma-related symptoms.
explanations.B: Renal dysfunction marks illness severity but is not itself an established independent risk factor for PTSD.
explanations.C: Routine peripheral venous access is not the type of invasive, distressing intervention linked to iatrogenic trauma.
explanations.D: Statin prescription at discharge has no relationship to the development of trauma-related symptoms.
explanations.E: ECMO support is an independent risk factor for PTSD, alongside ICU delirium, untreated pain, and other invasive procedures and devices.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman with a documented history of childhood sexual abuse requires a pelvic examination for abnormal bleeding. Before beginning, her physician tells her she may stop the examination at any point, asks whether she would prefer a chaperone in the room, and lets her decide when to start. She proceeds without distress. Which principle of trauma-informed care does this behavior best illustrate?

explanations.A: Choice refers to giving the patient meaningful control over how and when care proceeds, including the explicit option to decline or stop.
explanations.B: Collaboration refers to sharing decision-making about the treatment plan rather than granting control over the mechanics of a single encounter.
explanations.C: Empowerment refers to building on the patient's strengths and capacity for recovery over time.
explanations.D: Safety refers to establishing an environment that is physically and emotionally secure, such as a private and predictable clinical space.
explanations.E: Trustworthiness refers to transparency and consistency in what the clinician says and does, such as explaining findings honestly.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with posttraumatic stress disorder that developed after a prolonged ICU admission has missed his last four cardiology appointments and has not refilled his heart failure medications. He tells his primary care physician that he feels sick whenever he pulls into the hospital parking garage and turns around and drives home. He denies financial barriers, has reliable transportation, and says he wants to stay healthy. Which of the following best explains his behavior?

answers.A: Dissociative amnesia for the traumatic event
answers.B: Exaggerated startle response to unexpected stimuli
answers.D: Persistent avoidance of external reminders of the trauma
answers.E: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions

explanations.A: Dissociative amnesia describes an inability to recall an important aspect of the trauma, not active avoidance of a place.
explanations.B: An exaggerated startle response is a reflexive reaction to sudden stimuli and would not explain planned nonattendance at appointments.
explanations.C: Malingering requires an external incentive, and he denies benefit-seeking and states he wants to remain healthy.
explanations.D: Criterion C avoidance of external reminders such as places and situations is a major driver of treatment nonadherence in patients whose trauma occurred in a medical setting.
explanations.E: Inability to experience positive emotions is a Criterion D symptom and does not account for the specific hospital-triggered turnaround behavior.

questions.question: A 49-year-old male veteran with posttraumatic stress disorder has taken sertraline and prazosin for 6 months. His nightmares are less frequent, but he remains persistently fatigued, irritable, and unable to concentrate. His wife reports loud snoring and witnessed pauses in his breathing. BMI is 34 kg/m2 and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Polysomnography results are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.E: Refer for eye movement desensitization therapy

explanations.A: Mirtazapine may help sleep but does not treat the underlying airway obstruction and can promote further weight gain.
explanations.B: Prazosin is reducing his nightmares, and stopping it would remove an effective treatment without addressing the apneic events.
explanations.C: Dose escalation will not correct severe obstructive sleep apnea, which is the likely driver of his residual fatigue and irritability.
explanations.D: His apnea-hypopnea index of 38 events per hour indicates severe obstructive sleep apnea, and treating comorbid medical conditions such as OSA with CPAP has been shown to decrease PTSD symptoms.
explanations.E: Trauma-focused psychotherapy remains valuable, but it will not resolve symptoms driven by untreated severe sleep-disordered breathing.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with posttraumatic stress disorder after a house fire participates in a script-driven imagery study. She listens to a recorded narrative of the fire while physiologic measures are recorded, and she also demonstrates markedly increased heart rate responses to sudden loud tones compared with control subjects. The recorded data are shown. Which of the following best explains these findings?

answers.A: Baseline parasympathetic predominance at rest and during recall
answers.B: Blunted noradrenergic output during emotional recall of the event
answers.C: Impaired baroreceptor reflex sensitivity at rest and with stress
answers.D: Reduced facial electromyographic reactivity to trauma-related cues
answers.E: Sensitization of the autonomic nervous system acquired after trauma

explanations.A: Her data show sympathetic activation rather than parasympathetic predominance, with heart rate and skin conductance both rising sharply.
explanations.B: Noradrenergic activation is increased in PTSD, which is precisely what produces the rise in heart rate and skin conductance.
explanations.C: Baroreceptor dysfunction is not an established mechanism in PTSD and would not explain cue-specific reactivity to trauma imagery.
explanations.D: Facial EMG responding is increased rather than reduced, as shown by the rise in corrugator activity during imagery.
explanations.E: The best-replicated biologic finding in PTSD is heightened autonomic and facial EMG responding during trauma imagery and to trauma cues, and exaggerated heart rate responses to loud tones reflect acquired sensitization of the nervous system.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department 2 days after a motor vehicle collision in which her front-seat passenger died. She describes intrusive images of the crash, a sense of detachment from her surroundings, difficulty sleeping, an exaggerated startle response, and refusal to get back into a car. Her neurologic examination is normal, head CT is unremarkable, and toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following best explains why she does not currently meet criteria for acute stress disorder?

answers.A: Her exposure does not qualify as a traumatic event
answers.B: Her symptoms are better explained by a brief psychotic disorder
answers.C: Her symptoms have been present for fewer than 3 days
answers.D: Her symptoms have not yet persisted for more than 1 month
answers.E: She does not report amnesia for the traumatic event

explanations.A: Directly experiencing a collision in which another person was killed is a qualifying Criterion A exposure.
explanations.B: She has no delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech; detachment from surroundings is a dissociative symptom.
explanations.C: Acute stress disorder requires symptom persistence for at least 3 days after the trauma, and only 2 days have elapsed.
explanations.D: A duration of more than 1 month is the threshold for PTSD, not a requirement for acute stress disorder.
explanations.E: Dissociative amnesia is one of many qualifying symptoms and is not individually required for the diagnosis.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician 3 months after he was attacked by a neighbor's dog and required sutures. His mother reports that he repeatedly stages the attack with his stuffed animals, acting out the same sequence for hours at a time. He also wakes screaming from dreams he cannot describe and refuses to walk past the neighbor's yard. Which of the following symptom clusters does the repetitive play represent?

answers.C: Dissociative amnesia for the traumatic event
answers.E: Negative alterations in cognition and mood

explanations.A: Arousal symptoms include irritability, hypervigilance, startle, and sleep disturbance rather than reenactment of the event.
explanations.B: His refusal to walk past the neighbor's yard is the avoidance symptom; repetitive play is the opposite, an involuntary re-engagement with the trauma.
explanations.C: Dissociative amnesia describes an inability to recall an important aspect of the trauma, which the detailed reenactment argues against.
explanations.D: In children, repetitive play expressing aspects of the trauma is the developmental equivalent of recurrent intrusive memories under Criterion B, as are frightening dreams without recognizable content.
explanations.E: Negative alterations in cognition and mood include distorted self-blame, negative beliefs, detachment, and anhedonia.

questions.question: Two days after a mass casualty event at a manufacturing plant, the employer asks a consulting psychiatrist to deliver a mandatory single-session group debriefing to all 200 employees in order to prevent posttraumatic stress disorder. On screening, many employees are asymptomatic, while others report intrusive memories, insomnia, and difficulty concentrating. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

answers.A: Prescribe a short course of benzodiazepines to all exposed employees
answers.B: Provide the mandatory single-session group debriefing as requested
answers.C: Recommend against routine debriefing and offer CBT to symptomatic employees
answers.D: Refer all exposed employees for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing
answers.E: Start all exposed employees on sertraline as immediate prophylaxis

explanations.A: Benzodiazepines are classified as harmful in trauma-related disorders and have no role in universal prophylaxis.
explanations.B: Psychological debriefing and single-session techniques are not recommended because they appear ineffective and may increase symptoms in some settings.
explanations.C: Targeted cognitive-behavioral or supportive psychotherapy for symptomatic individuals may treat acute stress disorder and help prevent progression to PTSD, whereas universal debriefing is not recommended.
explanations.D: EMDR has not been established by controlled studies as an effective early or preventive intervention for acute stress disorder or PTSD.
explanations.E: Antidepressants may help patients with established symptoms but are not indicated as prophylaxis for an entire asymptomatic exposed population.
